summary: Primary NHTSA evidence supports certification/regulatory throughput as a distinct autonomy deployment constraint rather than a duplicate of technical driving capability. The distinction is visible at entity level: Zoox required exemptions for purpose-built noncompliant vehicles, while Tesla Cybercab is subject to an active NHTSA audit query over self-certification. Regulatory modernization is reducing the constraint, but not eliminating it; exemptions, FMVSS adaptation, objective AV performance standards and enforcement remain separate gates between autonomous capability and commercial scale.

materialFindings.finding: NHTSA states that automakers must certify vehicles against applicable FMVSS to access the U.S. market and opened an Audit Query on September 4, 2026 into Tesla's Cybercab self-certification after commercial deployment. This demonstrates that technical autonomous operation does not itself clear the certification gate.

NHTSA's Part 555 framework permits limited deployment of vehicles that do not fully comply with existing FMVSS, including purpose-built AVs without traditional controls, but requires an equivalent-safety showing and agency approval. This creates a regulatory throughput dependency distinct from ADS technical performance.

Zoox received an exemption pathway for its purpose-built driverless vehicles; NHTSA later allowed commercial deployment of up to 2,500 vehicles annually for two years under enhanced oversight. Entity-level exemption capacity can therefore bound deployment scale even when the underlying autonomy stack is operational.

NHTSA is simultaneously updating FMVSS for vehicles without human controls and funding first-ever AV performance standards. Constraint migration is therefore plausible: today's vehicle-design compliance/exemption bottleneck may gradually shift toward objective AV performance standards, safety-management evidence, first-responder interaction and post-crash behavior rather than disappear entirely.

proposedCanonicalChanges.proposal: Add a causal bottleneck concept for purpose-built AV certification/regulatory throughput, separate from core ADS technical capability, only after Chief/Beta confirms entity mapping and deduplicates it against any existing autonomy-regulation node.

suggestedNode.label: Purpose-built AV certification and exemption throughput

suggestedSignal.thesis: Commercial scaling of purpose-built AV fleets depends not only on ADS capability but also on certification, exemptions and evolving FMVSS/performance-standard pathways; regulatory modernization can reduce legacy equipment constraints while shifting scrutiny toward objective AV safety performance and operational oversight.
suggestedSignal.falsifier: Purpose-built AV fleets scale materially across U.S. jurisdictions without exemptions, self-certification disputes or certification-related deployment limits, while FMVSS modernization makes regulatory approval timing immaterial to commercial fleet growth for multiple years.

contradictions.issue: Regulation is both a constraint and an easing mechanism. Treating 'regulation' as uniformly negative would be wrong: NHTSA is actively removing legacy design barriers while retaining certification, exemption and enforcement gates.

unknowns: Long-run throughput and approval-time distribution for Part 555/AVEP applications under the streamlined process.
Whether future national AV performance standards materially compress entity-specific certification timelines or instead add a new evidence burden.
Company-specific economic sensitivity for active-universe autonomy names beyond the primary examples reviewed here.

peerRequests.request: Track NHTSA exemption grants, audit queries, FMVSS modernization and A2SCEND performance-standard milestones as non-score-moving weak signals until independently normalized and mapped.
For autonomy companies in the active universe, separate technical milestones from regulatory-certification milestones and quantify commercial dependence where primary filings permit.
Test the falsifier by searching for purpose-built AV programs scaling commercially without certification/exemption friction and for cases where regulation accelerated rather than delayed deployment.
